For a random variable X, the sub-gaussian tail, moment-growth, local quadratic-MGF, and bounded exponential-square-moment properties are equivalent up to absolute constant factors; property (iv) is the existence of K₄ > 0 such that E exp(X²/K₄²) ≤ 2.
A random variable satisfying one of Proposition 2.5.2(i)–(iv) is called sub-gaussian, and its sub-gaussian norm is defined by ‖X‖_{ψ₂} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2}.
Every sub-gaussian X satisfies P{|X| ≥ t} ≤ 2 exp(−c t²/‖X‖_{ψ₂}²) for all t ≥ 0, with an absolute constant c > 0.

source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.5.10, opening sentence and first displayed claim
source_evidence.observation: The exercise takes X₁, X₂, … to be a sequence of sub-gaussian random variables that are not necessarily independent and asks to show E max_i (|X_i|/√(1 + log i)) ≤ C K, where K = max_i ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂}.

The hint sets Y_i := X_i/(C K √(1 + log i)) with an absolute constant C chosen sufficiently large, applies the sub-gaussian tail bound (2.14) and a union bound to obtain P{∃i : |Y_i| ≥ t} ≲ exp(−t²) for t ≥ 1, and then invokes the integrated-tail formula split over [0,1] and [1,∞).

binders: A countably infinite sequence (X_i) indexed by i = 1, 2, … of real-valued random variables on a common probability space.
One absolute constant C > 0, independent of the sequence, its joint distribution, and the index i.
hypotheses: The variables X_i are not required to be independent.
No mean-zero or centering hypothesis is imposed.
definitions_and_conventions: A random variable X is sub-gaussian when it satisfies any of the equivalent properties (i)–(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2; equivalently for present purposes, there exists s > 0 such that E exp(X²/s²) ≤ 2.
Both occurrences of max_i in the displayed claim and in K range over every positive integer i.
The expectation is outside the countable maximum of the normalized absolute values; the normalized term is |X_i| divided by √(1 + log i).
The single constant C in the claimed estimate is absolute.
The hint uses the same normalization Y_i := X_i/(C K √(1 + log i)), Gaussian-type ψ₂ tails, a union bound over all indices, and integrated tails.
implicit_context: The joint maximum and the statement that independence is unnecessary implicitly require the sequence to be realized on one probability space.
The source uses the standard expectation and probability notation for real random variables.
The second displayed conclusion concerning max_{i≤N}|X_i| is outside this source-contract target.

details: The family is the countably infinite sequence X₁, X₂, …, not a fixed finite family.
The maximum in the target ranges over all positive integer indices.
Arbitrary dependence among the X_i is compatible with the claim.
The right-hand side is linear in K.
Each |X_i| is weighted by 1/√(1 + log i) before taking the maximum.
The expected value is taken after forming that maximum.
There is one universal multiplicative constant C in the conclusion.
C does not depend on i, the sequence, K, or any independence structure.
The normalization is chosen so that a union bound over the infinite index set is summable.
The hinted tail estimate is then integrated to bound the expected normalized maximum.

undebatable_constraints: The input is a countably infinite sequence X₁, X₂, ….
Every X_i is sub-gaussian in the sense of Definition 2.5.6.
K is written as max_i ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂}, not as a finite-N maximum or a different norm.
The left-hand side is E[max_i (|X_i|/√(1 + log i))].
The denominator depends on the same index i as X_i.
The bound is C K for one absolute constant C.
Only the first displayed claim of Exercise 2.5.10 is included; the subsequent finite-N deduction is not part of the target conclusion.

ambiguities.issue: The source writes max over a countably infinite index set without stating attainment.
ambiguities.evidence: Exercise 2.5.10 uses both max_i |X_i|/√(1 + log i) and K = max_i ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂} for X₁, X₂, ….
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must decide whether to preserve literal maximum language with an attainment condition or interpret the conventional infinite-family max as a supremum; replacing max by supremum is plausible but is not verbatim.

ambiguities.issue: The source does not explicitly assume that K is finite.
ambiguities.evidence: The exercise only defines K = max_i ‖X_i‖_{ψ₂}; individual sub-gaussianity makes each norm finite but does not by itself give a finite uniform maximum.
ambiguities.impact: For an unbounded family of ψ₂ norms the right-hand side may be infinite or the written maximum may fail to exist, so a finite-valued formal statement may need an explicit uniform boundedness assumption.

ambiguities.issue: The base of log is not stated in the selected passage.
ambiguities.evidence: The weight is printed as √(1 + log i) with no logarithm convention repeated nearby.
ambiguities.impact: Changing the logarithm base only changes absolute constant factors, but a formal target must select a concrete logarithm.

contract_plain_english: There is a universal constant C such that, for any countably infinite sequence of sub-gaussian real random variables on one probability space—even with arbitrary dependence—if K is the maximum of their ψ₂ norms, then the expected maximum over all positive integers i of |X_i| divided by √(1 + log i) is at most C K. Here the ψ₂ norm is inf {s > 0 : E exp(X²/s²) ≤ 2}. The source literally writes infinite maxima and does not separately state attainment or finiteness of K.
